Project Description: This project explores local queer history in Northern Virginia. It began as a class project in the Fall 2023 as a digital walking tour exploring sites of queer history in Alexandria, VA, with ArcGIS Storymaps. The project received support from the Alexandria Historical Society and the Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media to expand inquiry into Northern Virginia.
The complete project launched in Fall 2025, titled Out and About in Northern Virginia.
Collaborators: Hannah LeComte, George Mason University Alexandra Miller, George Mason University Ashleigh Williams, George Mason University Links: Out and About in Old Town Walking Tour Out and About in Northern Virginia

content: Project Description: Death by Numbers studies the Bills of Mortality, 17th century broadsides which published plague deaths in London. This project transcribed and published the information in these bills in a dataset for computational analysis.I worked on this project as a transcriber in the Fall of 2023. During this time, I also published a blog post titled Comparing the Bills of Mortality and Old Bailey Proceedings. In the spring of 2024, I rejoined the project and contributed to preliminary data visualizations, built with the JavaScript libraries Observable Plot and d3.js. Collaborators: Jessica Otis, George Mason University Jason Heppler, Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media Link: https://deathbynumbers.org/
summary: Project Description: Death by Numbers studies the Bills of Mortality, 17th century broadsides which published plague deaths in London.

Project Description: The Denig Manuscript explores the manuscript and watercolor paintings of Ludwig Denig (1755-1830), a shoemaker and apothecary living in Pennsylvania during the colonial and revolutionary eras. This website allows users to explore Denig's manuscript through a variety of ways: high resolution digital images, forensic report, music recordings, scholarly essays, and teaching materials. The document provides a window into the religious and cultural life of early Aemrica.In 2024, I contributed to The Denig Manuscript as a junior developer.
Collaborators: Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media Winterthur Museum, Garden & Library Link: The Denig Manuscript

Project Description: The American World War II Heritage Cities Program is a National Parks Service iniative that recognizes the contributions of everyday Americans to the homefront effort during World War II. Each state and territory can nominate one city or county for designation. The program highlights the how the war's impact on the cities and their populations, and creates educational material about the World War II homefront. In the summer of 2024, I interned with the American World War II Heritage Cities Program. My main task was constructing an interactive map to showcase the designated cities. After collecting open-source shapefiles of the cities, I created the spatial data layer using ArcGIS. I then used ArcGIS Experience Builder to build an interactive interface, combining the spatial data, city data, photographs, and brief descriptions of each city.
Collaborators: National Parks Service
Link: American World War II Heritage Cities

Project Description: World History Commons is an open-access, peer-reviewed educational resoruce for teachers. Its content focuses on world history teaching guides and primary sources. As a research assistant during the Fall of 2023, I reviewed websites and annotated primary sources. The website reviews accessed the pedagogical potential of the site, and how an educator could use it in their classroom. Similarly, primary source annotations focused on finding accessible digital sources, and providing brief context for them. This project aims to support world history teachers through accessible and usable material.Collaborators: Dr. Nate Sleeter, Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media
Link: My contributions to World History Commons

About Me I am a PhD student in History at George Mason University. Currently, I am a teaching assistant in the History Department, assisting with Introduction to Global History. Previously, as a graduate research assistant at the Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media, I did web development and data visualization for data-driven and digital public history projects. My broad research interests are 20th century United States, war and society, and digital history. I am currently researching the development of the Army Outdoor Recreation Program, its relation to the transition to the All-Volunteer Force, and American environmental culture.
I am originally from Salisbury, MD, and received my BA in History from Bridgewater College. When not doing history, I enjoy golfing, reading (fiction!), and live music.
